strengths: The paper proposes a simple, plug-and-play part-level correspondence prior (PartCo) that can be integrated into existing GCD methods without changing inference, and demonstrates consistent improvements across multiple baselines (SimGCD, SPTNet, FlipClass, SelEx) on fine-grained and generic benchmarks.

Extensive experiments cover multiple datasets (CUB, Stanford-Cars, FGVC-Aircraft, CIFAR10/100, ImageNet-100), backbones (DINOv2, DINOv3, CLIP), and ablations on label order, projection dimension, balancing factor, and unsupervised loss.
The constructed part labels are validated against CUB ground-truth part annotations, achieving 80.8% (1st order) and 77.5% (2nd order) accuracy, supporting their semantic quality.
The paper reports computational overhead and limitations honestly, and the method adds no inference cost.
weaknesses: The abstract and conclusion claim 'setting new benchmarks' for GCD, but on the SSB benchmark the best PartCo variant (85.5% All ACC) underperforms Hyp-SelEx (86.0%), and gains on generic datasets are marginal for some baselines (e.g., PartCo-SimGCD +0.3% average on CIFAR/ImageNet).

Equation 1 for the unsupervised contrastive loss contains a mathematical error: the numerator uses z_j' instead of z_i', making the positive pair undefined and inconsistent with standard contrastive learning.

The paper does not isolate why PartCo helps: since part labels are derived from the same frozen DINO features used to initialize the model, gains may stem from preserving frozen part structure rather than learning new part semantics. No comparison to a simple patch-feature distillation baseline is provided.

The choice between 1st- and 2nd-order part labels is dataset-dependent and heuristic; the paper does not specify a principled way to select the order for a new dataset, and it is unclear whether the order was tuned per dataset in the main results.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the candidate set for k in k-means, the exact architecture of the part projection head ψ_p, and the per-dataset order selection are not fully specified, and no code is released.

Comparison fairness is unclear: many competing GCD results in Tables 1 and 2 are reported with DINOv2/v3, but it is not stated whether these were reproduced under the same protocol or taken from original papers, which may advantage PartCo.
The method is limited to backbones with explicit patch tokens (ViTs), restricting applicability to CNN-based architectures, as acknowledged in the limitations.

strengths: The framework is genuinely plug-and-play: the part-level correspondence loss (L_pc) can be added to diverse GCD baselines (SimGCD, SPTNet, FlipClass, SelEx) without modifying architecture or inference, and the paper verifies this across all four baselines (Tables 1-2, Fig. 6).

The empirical evaluation is broad and consistent: three fine-grained SSB datasets, three generic datasets, two additional fine-grained datasets (Oxford-Pet, Herbarium19), and three backbones (DINOv2, DINOv3, CLIP). Improvements are reported in the same direction across essentially all settings.
The overhead analysis is honest and useful: training-only cost is modest (+5% time, +15% GFLOPs, no inference latency), and label construction time (5-180 min) is reported per dataset (Tables A-B).

Several targeted ablations strengthen the story: 1st vs 2nd order labels (Fig. 7, Table G), projection dimension (Table 3), balancing factor (Table 4), supervised vs unsupervised part losses (Fig. 8), and a foreground-only control that shows background masking alone does not explain the gains (Table I).

The paper provides an unusually thorough set of supporting analyses (per-class success/failure on CUB, comparison to CUB ground-truth part annotations in Table F, SD-DINOv2 label comparison in Table H, and K-estimation robustness in Tables J-K), and explicitly discusses limitations (Sec. S5).
weaknesses: Novelty is limited relative to prior part-based GCD work that the paper itself cites: SPTNet (spatial prompts), APL (part queries guided by DINO priors, replacing CLS with aggregated part representations), and PartGCD (GMM-based adaptive part decomposition with a part discrepancy regularizer). The claimed differentiator (a training-only supervisory signal that leaves the architecture/inference untouched) is a real but incremental distinction, and the paper does not demonstrate that its specific mechanism is superior to these alternatives beyond a single implicit-vs-explicit comparison (Table E).

The core mechanism is heuristic and under-justified. Part labels come from PCA (objectness threshold tau_obj=0.6) plus a second PCA mapped to RGB, then k-means where k* is chosen by maximizing min inter-centroid distance times a cluster-balance ratio. The candidate sweep set for k, the sensitivity to tau_obj, and why this objective should recover semantically meaningful parts are not established. Since the labels are derived from the *same* frozen DINOv2 features the model is then trained on, there is a real risk that L_pc acts mainly as a feature-space clustering/self-consistency regularizer rather than genuine cross-image 'correspondence.' The foreground-only ablation (Table I) is suggestive but does not rule this out, because it removes the clustering signal entirely rather than isolating it.

The headline claims are overstated. The abstract states PartCo is 'setting new benchmarks for GCD,' yet the strongest variant (PartCo-SelEx, 85.5 All on SSB with DINOv2) does not exceed Hyp-SelEx (86.0) in Table 1, and on generic benchmarks the gains are marginal (+0.3%/+0.9% for PartCo-SimGCD; +2.2%/+1.0% for PartCo-SelEx). The largest reported gains (+9.8%, +12.6%) are on the weakest baseline (SimGCD), whereas gains shrink sharply on strong baselines (SelEx: +2.4%), which is the opposite of what one would expect if the contribution addressed a fundamental limitation. The framing of 'outperforming most existing methods' is therefore only weakly supported by the strongest results.

Notational and reproducibility issues reduce clarity. The balancing factor is called lambda_b in Eq. 2 (balancing L_rep^u vs L_rep^s) and lambda_h in Eq. 8 (balancing L_pc^unsup vs L_pc^sup), yet the ablation in Table 4 labels the part-loss weight as lambda_b; it is unclear which weight is being swept and whether the two are tied. The k-sweep candidate range, the part-projection MLP specification, and the exact treatment of background patches (masked out or pooled) during aggregation are not fully specified in the main text.

The qualitative attention-map analysis (Sec. S3.2, Figs. C-D) is used to support the interpretation that PartCo focuses on discriminative parts, but it is purely visual and confounded: PartCo-SelEx and PartCo-SimGCD differ in their host baselines as well as in the part loss, so the differences cannot be attributed cleanly to PartCo. Combined with the borderline/marginal numbers on strong baselines, the evidential weight of this section is low.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant limitation of GCD methods: their reliance on global [CLS] representations and neglect of part-level cues. PartCo is well motivated and simple to integrate.

PartCo is plug-and-play: it adds a part-level contrastive loss without modifying the host GCD method's architecture or inference path, and experiments show consistent improvements for SimGCD, SPTNet, FlipClass, and SelEx across multiple datasets and backbones.

The empirical evaluation is extensive: SSB fine-grained datasets (CUB, Stanford-Cars, FGVC-Aircraft), generic datasets (CIFAR10/100, ImageNet-100), additional Oxford-Pet and Herbarium19, DINOv2/v3 and CLIP backbones, multiple ablations, K-estimation, computational overhead, and qualitative attention/failure analyses.

Ablations provide useful design insights: 1st-order labels work best for fine-grained datasets, 2nd-order labels help generic datasets, 3rd-order labels hurt; d'=128 is best; λ_b=0.35 is robust; foreground-only and implicit-vs-explicit comparisons help support the benefit of explicit part correspondence.

The constructed part labels are validated against CUB ground-truth parts (80.8% overall accuracy for 1st-order labels), and success/failure case analyses give concrete evidence about when part-level cues help.
The method is efficient at inference and introduces only modest training overhead (e.g., +2.5-5% training time, +15% GFLOPs, 8.6->12 GB peak memory in the reported setting).
weaknesses: The training objective is inconsistently presented. Eq. 8 defines L_total = L_gcd + L_pc with no overall weight on L_pc, but Table 4 and the implementation details describe a balancing factor λ_b weighting the part loss. λ_b is already used in Eq. 2 for the baseline representation loss, and λ_h in Eq. 8 is never specified. This makes the actual objective and hyperparameter settings unclear.

Reproducibility is weakened by missing details: no code link, unspecified candidate range for k* in the k-means sweep, unspecified MLP architecture for ψ_p, no value for λ_h, no description of how images with empty part sets P_c are handled, and no clarity on whether CLIP experiments construct part labels from CLIP or DINOv2 features.

The choice between 1st- and 2nd-order part labels is heuristic and qualitative ('subtle intra-class differences' vs 'pronounced inter-class differences'), not an automatic criterion, which reduces the method's plug-and-play practicality.

Key controls are missing to establish that part-level correspondence is the causal driver. There is no random/shuffled part-label control, and no patch-contrastive baseline without part grouping. The foreground-only ablation helps but does not fully rule out that gains come from additional contrastive regularization.

The part labels are derived from the same pretrained backbone that is then fine-tuned; the loss may partly act as a regularizer that preserves the initial DINOv2 patch structure rather than injecting new part knowledge. A cross-backbone label construction or frozen-backbone control would strengthen the claim.

The strongest results are not clearly state of the art. PartCo-SelEx is on par with Hyp-SelEx on SSB (85.5 vs 86.0 average All ACC) and below on Stanford-Cars (82.5 vs 83.8), so the abstract's 'setting new benchmarks' is overstated. Large gains are mostly over the weaker SimGCD baseline (+9.8% SSB), while gains over strong SelEx are modest (+2.4%).
Results are reported without multiple seeds or error bars, making small differences (e.g., generic-dataset gains of +0.3-2.2%) hard to interpret.
The main paper does not include an explicit limitations section; limitations are only in the supplementary material, and the impact statement is generic.

Novelty is incremental relative to existing part-based GCD methods (APL, PartGCD) and standard DINOv2 PCA-based part correspondence; the core technical components (PCA objectness, k-means part labels, supervised contrastive part loss) are largely off-the-shelf.
